VIDEO.title: The Hidden Meaning Behind the Wedding Feast
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 22:1-14 · Episode 43 (#46 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: Many are called, few are chosen
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 22:1-14. A king gives a wedding feast for his son and sends slaves to call those already invited, but they refuse. Some go off to their farms and business; others seize and kill the slaves. The king sends his armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city. Then he sends his slaves to the main highways to gather everyone they find, both evil and good, and the hall is filled. But one guest has no wedding clothes. Speechless, he is bound and thrown into the outer darkness. 'For many are called, but few are chosen.'

The leaders had just left (Mark 12:12), so the video thinks Jesus now speaks mainly to the crowds and disciples. Luke 14:16-24 tells a similar parable at a dinner. 'Called' means already invited: the first guests had accepted an invitation and then refused to come.

'Worthy' runs through Matthew: bear fruit worthy of repentance (3:8), a worthy house (10:11-13), and whoever loves family more than Jesus is not worthy of Him (10:37-38). Those gathered from the highways were both evil and good, like the wheat and tares.

The wedding clothes were provided; the guest refused to put them on. Isaiah 61:10 pictures God clothing His people with garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, the way a bridegroom puts on a priest-like headdress. Zephaniah 1:8 warns of punishment on all who clothe themselves with foreign garments: idolatry and mixed allegiance.
The lesson: to be worthy of God's kingdom, you must remove all your idols and foreign allegiances and allow the Lord to fully consecrate, or fully clothe, you with His righteousness.
QUOTES: To be worthy of God's kingdom, you must remove all your idols and foreign allegiances and allow the Lord to fully consecrate or fully clothe you with his righteousness.
The proper clothes were made available to him, but he refused to put them on.
It's not about the man's clothes at all. It's about his refusal to change.
In Zephaniah, your clothes represent your allegiance.

LSB_QUOTES.text: The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son.
For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness,
For many are called, but few are chosen.

src.text: And he sent out his slaves to call those who had been called to the wedding feast, and they were unwilling to come. Again he sent out other slaves saying, ‘Tell those who have been called, “Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my oxen and my fattened livestock are all butchered and everything is ready; come to the wedding feast.”’ But they paid no attention and went their way, one to his own farm, another to his business,

lines.text: 'Called' means they were already invited and had said yes. When the feast was ready, they refused to come.
Some just got distracted by farm and business. Others seized and killed the slaves, as the vine-growers did in the last parable (21:35).

The rabbis told a similar parable: 'The situation is comparable to a king who invited his servants to a feast and did not set a time for them to come' (Talmud Shabbat 153a), credited to Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai.

left.text: Then he *said to his slaves, ‘The wedding is ready, but those who were called were not worthy.

right.text: Therefore bear fruit in keeping with repentance;

lines.text: Worthiness runs through Matthew: fruit in keeping with repentance (3:8), a worthy house (10:11-13), and 'he who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me' (10:37).
'Set their city on fire' (22:7) has long been read as a picture of Jerusalem's fall in AD 70.

src.text: Go therefore to the main highways, and as many as you find there, call to the wedding feast.’ And those slaves went out into the streets and gathered together all they found, both evil and good; and the wedding hall was filled with dinner guests.

lines.text: The main roads are where the poor and outsiders gather. The invitation goes to everyone.
'Both evil and good' sounds like the wheat and tares: until the end, the gathered people are mixed (13:41-42).
Luke's dinner parable sends the slave for 'the poor and crippled and blind and lame' (Luke 14:21).

src.text: “But when the king came in to look over the dinner guests, he saw a man there who was not dressed in wedding clothes, and he *said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here without wedding clothes?’ And the man was speechless. Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness; in that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

lines.text: The guests came straight from the roads, so the king must have provided the garments. This man was given the clothes; he refused to put them on.
He has no answer. He is speechless because he has no excuse.

src.text: I will rejoice greatly in Yahweh; / My soul will rejoice in my God, / For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness, / As a bridegroom decks himself with a headdress, / And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

lines.text: The wedding garment is righteousness that God provides. In Isaiah 61:10 the word for 'decks' (kahan) is related to the word for priest: the bridegroom dresses like a priest.
God clothes His people in Ezekiel 16:10 too. In Eden, Adam and Eve made fig-leaf coverings (Genesis 3:7), but Yahweh God made garments of skin and clothed them (3:21).

left.text: Be silent before Lord Yahweh! / For the day of Yahweh is near, / For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice; / He has set apart His guests.

right.text: “Then it will be on the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice / That I will punish the princes, the king’s sons, / And all who clothe themselves with foreign garments.

lines.text: Zephaniah's feast has invited guests too, and judgment on those dressed in foreign clothes. The context (1:4-6) is Baal worship and swearing by Milcom alongside Yahweh: mixed allegiance.
Giving allegiance to the Lord and to idols at the same time is syncretism, and the first commandment rejects it: 'You shall have no other gods before Me' (Exodus 20:3).
Zephaniah also calls Jerusalem's judges 'wolves at evening' (Zephaniah 3:3), which the video links to the wolves in sheep's clothing of Matthew 7:15.

left.text: For many are called, but few are chosen.”

right.text: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.

lines.text: Many accept the invitation; fewer let God clothe them completely. A double-minded person is 'unstable in all his ways' (James 1:8).
Halakha, Jewish law, comes from the verb 'to walk,' and the first believers were called 'the Way' (Acts 9:2). The garment is a way of life.

BACKGROUND.p: In the ancient world a host often sent an invitation in advance and then a second call when the meal was ready. Refusing the second call after accepting the first was a public insult.

The Talmud credits Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai with a parable of a king's feast with no set time: 'The wise among them entered before him adorned in their finest clothes, and the fools entered before him dirty' (Talmud Shabbat 153a). There the clothes stand for readiness through repentance.

In Scripture clothing often marks status and loyalty: priestly garments, mourning sackcloth, the robe given to the returning son (Luke 15:22). Zephaniah's 'foreign garments' shows clothing could signal foreign worship.

DEBATES.p: There is no clear first-century evidence that hosts supplied wedding clothes, though some point to royal gifts of robes (2 Kings 10:22). Many read the point as the guest's refusal, whoever supplied the clothing.
Readers have taken it as imputed righteousness, as a changed life (Chrysostom), or both. The video combines them: God clothes, and the guest must not wear anything foreign.
Many see 22:7 as a picture of AD 70; others see a stock feature of royal punishment stories.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Wolves in sheep's clothing are in Matthew 7:15-16; the video says 17:15-16.
The video gives the Jewish levels of reading as peshat, remez and sod; the usual list is four (peshat, remez, derash, sod), and the acronym PaRDeS is medieval.
Fig-leaf coverings are Adam and Eve's own work (Genesis 3:7); God clothes them in 3:21.
Matthew 22:1 says Jesus 'spoke to them again,' and 22:15 shows the Pharisees still near, so whether the audience changed after Mark 12:12 is debated.
That the king supplied the wedding garments is an inference; the parable does not say it.

QUESTIONS: Why would people who accepted an invitation refuse to come when the feast was ready?
What 'farms and businesses' most easily distract you from God's call?
How do Genesis 3:21 and Isaiah 61:10 shape your picture of the wedding clothes?
What 'foreign garments' or mixed allegiances are common today?
How do grace and diligence fit together in Chrysostom's comment?
What does it mean for you to be fully clothed by God this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: to be worthy of God's kingdom, you must remove all your idols and foreign allegiances and allow the Lord to fully consecrate or fully clothe you with His righteousness. In Zephaniah, your clothes represent your allegiance; if your allegiance is to the one true God, it cannot be to anyone or anything else. God's covering of His people is relational and covenantal, going back to Eden. The man in the parable had the proper clothes made available and refused to put them on. No one can serve two masters, and a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): list one loyalty that competes with God for your time or trust. Pray Isaiah 61:10 over it this week and take one concrete step to set it aside.

## Key people
- The king: God the Father, who gives the feast for His Son. [Background] Compare the king in the parable of 18:23.
- The son: Jesus, the bridegroom. [Background] Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom in 9:15.
- The slaves: The prophets and messengers sent to call the guests. [Background] Mistreated and killed, like the slaves in 21:35-36.
- Those who were called: Invited, but unwilling; the leaders and those who rejected Him. [Background] Luke's version has excuses about a field, oxen and a wife (Luke 14:18-20).
- The guests from the highways: Evil and good, the poor and outsiders. [Background] Compare Luke 14:21-23.
- The man without wedding clothes: Accepted the call but refused the garment provided. [Background] The king calls him 'Friend' (22:12), as the landowner did in 20:13.

## Places [Background]
- Temple (named in the video): Jesus is teaching in the temple courts (21:23; 22:1).
- Antonia Fortress: Roman garrison beside the temple; in AD 70 Titus's legions took it first.
- Upper City: Wealthy quarter, burned in AD 70.

## Key terms
- Wedding feast: A celebration that could last days; here a picture of the messianic banquet.
- Called: Invited; in 22:14 'called' (klētos) is set against 'chosen' (eklektos).
- Wedding clothes: Festive clothing for the feast; in the video, righteousness that God provides.
- Foreign garments: In Zephaniah 1:8, clothing tied to foreign worship and loyalties.
- Syncretism: Mixing the worship of the true God with other gods or loyalties.
- Halakha: Jewish law and practice; from the Hebrew verb 'to walk.'

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- γάμος gamos (G1062, Greek): Wedding, wedding feast. (Matt 22:2, 8)
- ἔνδυμα endyma (G1742, Greek): Garment, clothing. (Matt 22:11, 12)
- φιμόω phimoō (G5392, Greek): To muzzle, silence; 'speechless.' (Matt 22:12)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Two invitations: In the ancient world a host often sent an invitation in advance and then a second call when the meal was ready. Refusing the second call after accepting the first was a public insult.
- A rabbinic parallel: The Talmud credits Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai with a parable of a king's feast with no set time: 'The wise among them entered before him adorned in their finest clothes, and the fools entered before him dirty' (Talmud Shabbat 153a). There the clothes stand for readiness through repentance.
- Garments and identity: In Scripture clothing often marks status and loyalty: priestly garments, mourning sackcloth, the robe given to the returning son (Luke 15:22). Zephaniah's 'foreign garments' shows clothing could signal foreign worship.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For the garment is life and practice." Homilies on Matthew 69, on 22:11-13. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "although to be called and to be cleansed was of grace, yet, when called and clothed in clean garments, to continue keeping them so, this is of the diligence of them that are called." Homilies on Matthew 69, on 22:11-14. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who provided the garment? There is no clear first-century evidence that hosts supplied wedding clothes, though some point to royal gifts of robes (2 Kings 10:22). Many read the point as the guest's refusal, whoever supplied the clothing.
- What is the garment? Readers have taken it as imputed righteousness, as a changed life (Chrysostom), or both. The video combines them: God clothes, and the guest must not wear anything foreign.
- Is the city Jerusalem? Many see 22:7 as a picture of AD 70; others see a stock feature of royal punishment stories.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Wolves in sheep's clothing are in Matthew 7:15-16; the video says 17:15-16.
- The video gives the Jewish levels of reading as peshat, remez and sod; the usual list is four (peshat, remez, derash, sod), and the acronym PaRDeS is medieval.
- Fig-leaf coverings are Adam and Eve's own work (Genesis 3:7); God clothes them in 3:21.
- Matthew 22:1 says Jesus 'spoke to them again,' and 22:15 shows the Pharisees still near, so whether the audience changed after Mark 12:12 is debated.
- That the king supplied the wedding garments is an inference; the parable does not say it.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why would people who accepted an invitation refuse to come when the feast was ready?
2. What 'farms and businesses' most easily distract you from God's call?
3. How do Genesis 3:21 and Isaiah 61:10 shape your picture of the wedding clothes?
4. What 'foreign garments' or mixed allegiances are common today?
5. How do grace and diligence fit together in Chrysostom's comment?
6. What does it mean for you to be fully clothed by God this week?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: to be worthy of God's kingdom, you must remove all your idols and foreign allegiances and allow the Lord to fully consecrate or fully clothe you with His righteousness. In Zephaniah, your clothes represent your allegiance; if your allegiance is to the one true God, it cannot be to anyone or anything else. God's covering of His people is relational and covenantal, going back to Eden. The man in the parable had the proper clothes made available and refused to put them on. No one can serve two masters, and a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.
- Study note (added): list one loyalty that competes with God for your time or trust. Pray Isaiah 61:10 over it this week and take one concrete step to set it aside.
